name: Serdev suture

card.summary: A needle-suture thread lifting method from the suspension-thread family, with thin published evidence on the specific technique.
card.note: Early sutures increased inflammatory reaction; threads can be hard to remove.

quick.overview:
The Serdev suture is a thread-lift technique in which sutures are placed under the skin to hold sagging tissue up, rather than cutting out skin. It is associated with a surgeon named Serdev.

The sources available are thin: a general review of suspension threads and a general encyclopedia entry on thread lifts. No studies specific to the Serdev technique were found.
quick.mechanism: The sources describe suture threads placed in the dermis and subcutis to lift lax tissue; they do not detail the Serdev needle method.
quick.risks: A 2016 review reports that early sutures increased inflammatory reaction. A general reference notes that threads can be difficult to remove and that practitioner training varies.

lead: The Serdev suture is a needle-based suture-lifting technique for facial rejuvenation, associated with a surgeon named Serdev, who introduced a polycaproamide suture used for facial lifting. [1] It belongs to the family of suspension or thread lifts, in which sutures placed under the skin hold sagging tissue in a higher position without cutting out skin. [1][2]

People consider thread lifts to lift the midface, jowls and neck and sharpen facial contours with less recovery time than a surgical facelift. [1][2] A 2016 review of suspension threads says Sulamanidze and colleagues began using polypropylene threads after Serdev introduced a polycaproamide suture, and that these early sutures increased inflammatory reaction. [1] The same review presents polydioxanone as a current option for antiaging treatment with a low rate of adverse reactions. [1]
No published study specific to the Serdev technique was located; the available literature covers thread lifts in general.

chain: Sutures are placed in the dermis and subcutis
Tissue is held in a higher position

angle.text: Suspension sutures raise lax facial tissue to restore contour and reduce sagging, offering a lift that requires fewer incisions and shorter recovery than a conventional facelift. [1][2]

infobox: Polypropylene, then polydioxanone in current practice [1]

paras: Suture threads are described as a minimally invasive technique for facial rejuvenation that uses absorbable and non-absorbable sutures placed in the dermis and subcutis to lift lax tissue, with fewer incisions and shorter recovery than conventional facelifts. [1] Wikipedia describes thread lifts as a non-surgical facelift in which barbed threads pull the skin of the face and neck upward without removing skin, and says combining threads with other rejuvenation methods gives better results. [2]

The 2016 review credits Serdev with introducing a polycaproamide suture for facial lifting, followed by Sulamanidze and colleagues using polypropylene threads for thread lifts. [1] Wikipedia names the anti-ptosis (APTOS) thread lift as one named variant of the broader family. [2]

The 2016 review notes that early sutures increased inflammatory reaction. [1] Wikipedia says the results of thread lifts can be very good but that the procedure can also cause irreversible damage, and quotes cosmetic doctor Vincent Wong describing it as potentially the most dangerous procedure an aesthetic practitioner can perform because the threads stay in the skin and cannot easily be removed. [2]

A 2021 BBC investigation, summarised on Wikipedia, found 26 cosmetic training academies in Liverpool offering courses of a few hours to a few days, and an undercover nurse filmed a thread-lift course with poor infection control; in the UK, practitioners performing thread lifts are not required to hold mandatory qualifications. [2]

No studies found specific to the Serdev suture. A 2016 narrative review covers suspension threads in general, including several suture materials. [1] A retrospective study of 100 patients who had insoluble thread lifts (a different thread type) found the rejuvenation effect decreased during the first year and then increased, and rose with the number of threads and procedures. [3]
